**All solutions.**

**1. If $\alpha>1$:** exactly the linear functions
$$\boxed{\,f(n)=cn\quad(n\in\mathbb N^+),\quad c\in\mathbb R\text{ arbitrary}\,}$$

**2. If $0<\alpha<1$:** choose arbitrary $c=a$ and arbitrary $a_n\in\mathbb R$ $(n\ge2)$, and put
$$f(n)=\begin{cases}a,&n=1,\\[2pt] a_n,&n\ge2\text{ (arbitrary)},\end{cases}\qquad\text{with the sole requirement }f(2)=2a\text{ replaced by }a_2=2a;$$
i.e. $f(1)=a$, $f(2)=2a$, and $f(n)$ arbitrary for each $n\ge3$.

**3. If $\alpha=1$:** choose arbitrary $c=a$ and arbitrary $a_n\in\mathbb R$ for odd $n\ge3$; then
$$f(2m)=2m\,a\ (\forall m\ge1),\qquad f(1)=a,\qquad f(n)=a_n\ (\text{odd }n\ge3\text{ arbitrary}).$$

Every function of these forms satisfies $f(k+m)=f(k)+f(m)$ whenever $\alpha m\le k\le(\alpha+1)m$, and there are no others.

All such functions are of the form
\[
\boxed{f(n)=cn\quad(n\in\mathbb N^+,\ c\in\mathbb R)}
\]
for every α > 0. If α ≤ 1 this is the complete answer. If α > 1, write q=⌊(α+1)(α+2)⌋ and let d_α be the set of integers d with ⌈(α+1)(α+2)/2⌉ < d < ⌊α⌋(α+2) (d_α=∅ if α is an integer); then f(n)=cn for all n∉d_α (mod q), and f may take arbitrary values on the classes n≡d (mod q), d∈d_α, independently of c. (For integer α≥2 the set d_α is empty, so f(n)=cn.)
